title: Short Stuff: Backyard Burials
summary: Short Stuff episode on backyard burials. Josh and Chuck open with banter about their own after-death wishes and Chuck's decision to bury his cat Lauren in his backyard. They then discuss that burying relatives on your own land is legal in many US states (with California, Washington State, Indiana and Washington D.C. named as restrictive, and Virginia mentioned), while other states allow it only if you own enough land. Topics include resale concerns, setbacks from water and property lines, state rules on taking possession of a body within about 24 hours without embalming or refrigeration, the need to file a death certificate with the county clerk within about five days, burial depth (six feet as a rule of thumb, New Mexico the only state requiring six feet, New Jersey four feet, most states between eighteen inches and four feet), and the requirement to record the burial site with a cemetery commission so the land is treated as a cemetery.

segments.title: Opening banter on after-death wishes and burying a cat
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck talk about their own wishes for what happens to their bodies after death. Chuck says he buried his cat Lauren in the backyard. They joke about what would happen if the pet were a human relative.

segments.title: Legality of burying relatives on your own land
segments.summary: The hosts explain that burying family members on your own land is legal in many states, while California, Washington State, Indiana and Washington D.C. restrict it, with Virginia also mentioned. Where it is allowed, owners generally need enough land. They warn that a future sale of the property could be affected by a grave on it.

segments.title: Setbacks and site rules
segments.summary: The hosts say local rules vary by state, county or district. Burial sites must be set back from property lines, streams and water tables, and from buildings and neighboring properties, to protect the water supply.

segments.title: Taking possession of a body and skipping embalming
segments.summary: In some states a relative can take a body from a hospital and bury it at home without a funeral director. Embalming is not required by law in many states. If burial happens within about 24 hours, embalming and refrigeration may not be needed. The hosts suggest digging the grave first.

segments.title: Easements, funeral director rules and death certificates
segments.summary: Owners may need to provide public access to the grave site through an easement. Some states require a funeral director, while others allow family to handle things. A death certificate must still be filed, typically within about five days, and county clerk office hours can delay filing. A funeral director can file electronically.

segments.title: Burial depth and the six-foot rule
segments.summary: The six-foot rule is not the law in most places. New Mexico is the only US state where backyard burial is legal and requires six feet. New Jersey requires four feet, and most states fall between eighteen inches and four feet. Shallow graves speed decomposition but risk scavengers and odor. Chuck says he buried Lauren a couple of feet deep above hard clay.

segments.title: Recording the land as a cemetery
segments.summary: Burying someone on private land legally makes that portion a cemetery, which brings anti-desecration and cemetery laws, some dating back to Roman times. The burial must be recorded with the local cemetery or commission that keeps grave records.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up, suggesting listeners look into the laws before considering a backyard burial.
